elements.quote: Abstract: Mucormycosis, a secondary fungal infection, gained much attention in the ongoing COVID19 pandemic.... This study aims to compute the pooled prevalence of CAM and other associated clinical outcomes.... This meta-analysis comprised six studies...
elements.reason: The document title and the abstract explicitly identify the work as a systematic review/meta-analysis and the abstract language refers to 'This meta-analysis' and 'This study aims' indicating a systematic review.

elements.quote: This study aims to compute the pooled prevalence of CAM and other associated clinical outcomes.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the primary objective/review question: to compute pooled prevalence of CAM and associated outcomes.

elements.quote: All studies reporting the prevalence of mucormycosis among COVID-19 patients were eligible for inclusion.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main inclusion criterion but does not specify exclusion criteria or fuller details of eligibility in the abstract.

elements.quote: MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, and WHO COVID-19 databases were scanned to retrieve the relevant articles until August 2021.
elements.reason: The abstract lists the information sources used and reports the date until which they were searched (August 2021).

elements.quote: Two investigators independently screened the articles against the selection criteria, extracted the data, and performed the quality assessment using the JBI tool.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method/tool used for risk-of-bias/quality assessment (JBI tool) and that two investigators performed quality assessment.

elements.quote: The pooled prevalence of CAM was the primary outcome, and the pooled prevalence of diabetes, steroid exposure, and the mortality rate were the secondary outcomes of interest. Comprehensive Meta-Analysis software version 2 was used for performing the meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The abstract indicates that a meta-analysis was performed and names the software used, specifying that pooled prevalence was computed (methods of synthesis).

elements.quote: This meta-analysis comprised six studies with a pooled sample size of 52,916 COVID-19 patients with a mean age of 62.12 ± 9.69 years.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and participants and provides key study characteristics (mean age).

elements.quote: The pooled prevalence of CAM (seven cases per 1000 patients) was 50 times higher than the highest recorded background of mucormycosis (0.14 cases per 1000 patients). A high mortality rate was found among CAM patients with a pooled prevalence rate of 29.6% (95% CI: 17.2-45.9%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for main outcomes (pooled prevalence and mortality) and provides summary estimates (and a CI for mortality); it also contextualizes the prevalence result.

elements.quote: The pooled prevalence of CAM (seven cases per 1000 patients) ... A high mortality rate was found among CAM patients with a pooled prevalence rate of 29.6% (95% CI: 17.2-45.9%).
elements.reason: A meta-analysis summary estimate is reported for outcomes; a confidence interval is provided for the mortality estimate but the abstract does not provide a confidence interval for the primary pooled CAM prevalence estimate.

The abstract does not report any comparisons between groups or indicate group-favoring directions; the review focuses on prevalence estimates rather than group comparisons, so this item does not apply.
The abstract contains no brief summary of important limitations (risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision) of the included evidence.

elements.quote: Optimal glycemic control and the judicious use of steroids should be the approach for tackling rising CAM cases.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of results and an implication/recommendation based on the findings.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide a register name or registration number for the review.

No retrieved text explicitly describes the current state of knowledge about COVID-19-associated mucormycosis or outlines important uncertainties in the literature. Available chunks describe methods, living review process, strengths, and implications, but do not summarize existing knowledge or key knowledge gaps.

elements.quote: Aliving systematic review is a form of evidence synthesis which is updated regularly when sufficient new evidence becomes available [60]. Two reviewers will independently search the updated published and unpublished evidence every six months and include all relevant articles as per the previously described inclusion criteria. The meta-analysis will be updated continuously depending on the availability of new evidence and will be published as a separate publication.
elements.reason: This text explains the rationale and need for conducting a living systematic review/meta-analysis (regular updates as new evidence becomes available) and justifies why the review will be updated.
No retrieved evidence discusses existing similar systematic reviews, nor cites or explains the need relative to prior reviews or updates/replications.
The review is a prevalence/meta-analysis of an infectious complication (CAM), not a review of intervention effects; a mechanism of action for an intervention is not relevant.
The review does not assess complex interventions or delivery contexts and does not present or require a logic model; this item is not applicable.

elements.quote: The primary outcome of this meta-analysis was to compute the pooled global prevalence of CAM. The secondary outcome was to compute the pooled prevalence of diabetes, steroid use, and mortality among CAM patients.
elements.reason: The review's objectives (primary and secondary outcomes) are explicitly stated, but they are not presented using a recognized question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO) as required by this element.

elements.quote: The primary outcome of this meta-analysis was to compute the pooled global prevalence of CAM. The secondary outcome was to compute the pooled prevalence of diabetes, steroid use, and mortality among CAM patients.
elements.reason: This review addresses prevalence outcomes rather than intervention effects, so planned comparisons using PICO (for intervention reviews) do not apply.

elements.quote: We included cross-sectional or longitudinal studies reporting the prevalence of mucormycosis among confirmed COVID-19 patients (based on RT-PCR reports). Only studies with confirmed mucormycosis cases diagnosed based on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention criteria, i.e., either through the histopathology, culture, or staining techniques among COVID-19 patients, were qualified for inclusion. Case reports, case series, reviews or studies with incomplete information about the confirmed number of mucormycosis cases from the total number of COVID-19 patients were excluded.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies eligible study designs, case definitions for COVID-19 and mucormycosis, and types of reports excluded, but does not explicitly report settings or any follow-up requirements, so the description of all study characteristics is incomplete.
No information is provided in the retrieved evidence about report-level eligibility restrictions (e.g., years, languages, or publication/report status).

elements.quote:
Records excluded = 09
Outcome not of interest = 7
Study design not of interest = 2
elements.reason: The flowchart shows exclusions for 'Outcome not of interest' (i.e., outcomes not measured), but there is no explicit distinction or mention of exclusions because outcome results were not reported; evidence does not demonstrate both categories being distinguished.

elements.quote: The subgroup analysis was performed based on diabetes as a comorbidity, and steroid exposure.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies groups used in syntheses (subgroup analyses by diabetes and steroid exposure), linking these groups to analytic comparisons in the meta-analysis.
No rationale is provided in the retrieved evidence explaining notable restrictions on study eligibility (e.g., why certain designs or report types were excluded).

elements.quote: We extensively searched the following databases: MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, and the WHO COVID-19 database until 16 August 2021.
elements.reason: The report states the date (16 August 2021) up to which the listed information sources were searched.

elements.quote: We extensively searched the following databases: MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, and the WHO COVID-19 database until 16 August 2021.
elements.reason: Database names and interfaces (e.g., MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid)) are reported, and a search date is given, but available coverage dates for each database are not reported.

elements.quote: We extensively searched the following databases: MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, and the WHO COVID-19 database until 16 August 2021.
elements.reason: Names of study registers/online repositories searched (Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, WHO COVID-19 database) and the search date are provided, but any date restrictions specific to those registers are not reported.
No websites, search engines or URLs are reported in the evidence; URLs and names (beyond database names) are not provided.
There is no mention of contacting organisations or manufacturers to identify studies.
No evidence describes types of individuals (e.g., experts, authors) contacted to identify studies.

elements.quote: The bibliography of relevant reviews was hand searched for any additional articles, followed by citation tracking of all the relevant articles.
elements.reason: The authors specify that bibliographies of relevant reviews were hand-searched (i.e., the type of reference lists examined).

elements.quote: The bibliography of relevant reviews was hand searched for any additional articles, followed by citation tracking of all the relevant articles.
elements.reason: Backward/forward citation searching (citation tracking) is reported, but the seed reports, citation index/platform used, and the date(s) when citation searching was performed are not specified.
The manuscript does not report consulting journals or conference proceedings as separate sources; no evidence that this item applies.

elements.quote: The search strategy comprised medical subject heading terms related to coronavirus such as coronavirus* OR corona virus* OR 2019-ncov OR ncov19 OR ncov-19 OR 2019novel CoV OR SARS-CoV2 OR SARS-CoV-2 OR sarscov2 OR sarscov-2 OR SARS-2nCoV OR SARS-2-Cov OR SARS-CoV-19 OR Sars-coronavirus2 OR Sars-coronavirus-2 OR SARS 2 coronavirus* OR Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome-CoV-2 OR SARS-like coronavirus* OR coronavirus-19 OR covid19 OR COVID-19 OR COVID 2019, and mucormycosis such as mucormycosis OR mucormycoses OR mucormycose OR mucoromycosis OR mucoromycoses OR zygomycosis OR zygomycoses OR 'black fungus' OR 'black fungi' OR Mucorales OR mucoralean OR Absidia OR Cunninghamella OR Mortierella OR Mucor OR Apophysomyces OR Saksenaea OR Rhizopus OR Rhizomucor OR Lichtheimia OR Cokeromyces OR Actinomucor OR Syncephalastrum (Supplementary File S2).
elements.reason: Provides an explicit search string/terms used (covers COVID-19 and mucormycosis terms) but does not present the complete, per-database search strategies as actually run for every database/register/website — instead refers to Supplementary File S2 and does not show separate strategies or syntaxes for each source.

elements.quote: The literature search conducted in August 2021 aimed to find both published and unpublished studies. ... The literature search was not restricted to any language. We extensively searched the following databases: MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, and the WHO COVID-19 database until 16 August 2021.
elements.reason: Reports some limits (search date up to 16 August 2021 and no language restriction) but does not fully describe or justify all search limits in relation to eligibility criteria (no rationale provided for date range or other potential filters).
No citation of published search approaches or filters nor description of adaptations is present in the provided evidence.
No mention of use of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools to identify or refine search terms in the provided evidence.
No tools used to translate search strings between sources are specified in the provided evidence.
No description of any validation of the search strategy (process or validation studies) is present in the provided evidence.
No information about peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) or the peer-review process/tool is provided in the available evidence.
There is no description of the final conceptual structure or explorations used to develop the search (e.g., if not based on PICO) in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Two reviewers (S.H. and A.R.) independently scanned all the retrieved articles initially based on title and abstract, followed by full-text readings in the later phase.
elements.reason: The manuscript states the number of reviewers (two) who performed screening at the title/abstract stage and refers to subsequent full-text readings.

elements.quote: Two reviewers (S.H. and A.R.) independently scanned all the retrieved articles initially based on title and abstract, followed by full-text readings in the later phase.
elements.reason: Independence of reviewers is explicitly reported for the initial title/abstract screening, but independence is not explicitly stated for the full-text screening stage.

elements.quote: The reviewers tried to resolve any confusion in the study selection process through discussion; if consensus was not reached by discussion, then the decision was made by consulting a third reviewer (M.K.).
elements.reason: The process for resolving screening disagreements (discussion, then consulting a third reviewer) is described.
No information is provided about contacting study investigators to obtain or confirm eligibility information.
No methods for translating abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment are reported.
No automation tools or their integration into the selection process are mentioned in the manuscript, indicating this element does not apply.
No externally derived classifiers or pre-screening classifiers are described or mentioned, so this element does not apply.
No internally derived classifiers, their training, or validation are reported, so this element does not apply.
No mention of machine-learning prioritisation tools or stopping/prioritisation rules; element does not apply.
No use of crowdsourcing platforms for study selection is reported; element does not apply.
No previously screened datasets used to eliminate records are described; element does not apply.

elements.quote: Two independent reviewers (S.H. and H.B.) extracted the following information from all the eligible studies: study author, year, country, study period or duration, the number of COVID-19 cases, confirmation of COVID-19, the diagnosis of mucormycosis, the number of mucormycosis cases among COVID-19 patients, the presence of comorbidities, the mean age of mucormycosis patients, female (%), clinical symptoms, treatment modalities, and mortality.
elements.reason: Explicit statement that two independent reviewers (S.H. and H.B.) extracted data from eligible studies.

elements.quote: Two independent reviewers (S.H. and H.B.) extracted the following information from all the eligible studies: ...
elements.reason: States that two reviewers were independent, indicating multiple data collectors worked independently.

elements.quote: Any confusion in the data collection process was resolved by discussion with a third reviewer (M.K.).
elements.reason: Describes the process for resolving disagreements by discussion with a third reviewer (M.K.).
No description found of processes to obtain or confirm data from study investigators.
No information provided about use, training, or validation of automation tools for data collection.
No methods reported for translating articles during data collection (although search was not language-restricted, translation methods are not described).
No software or tools described for extracting data from figures.
No decision rules described for selecting data from multiple reports or resolving inconsistencies beyond general reviewer discussion/third reviewer consultation.

elements.quote: The primary outcome of this meta-analysis was to compute the pooled global prevalence of CAM. The secondary outcome was to compute the pooled prevalence of diabetes, steroid use, and mortality among CAM patients.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists the primary and secondary outcome domains (global CAM prevalence; prevalence of diabetes, steroid use, and mortality among CAM patients) but does not provide formal definitions of these outcomes (e.g., case definitions, diagnostic criteria, or denominators), so outcomes are listed but not fully defined.

No explicit specification of the time frame of measurement for each outcome domain (for example timing of mortality measurement, timepoints, or follow-up periods) is provided in the retrieved evidence.
The manuscript does not state whether all results compatible with each outcome domain (e.g., all measures, time points, or analyses) were sought.
There is no description of a process used to select among multiple compatible results within outcome domains (this is conditional on e3 and evidence for any selection process is not reported).
No report of changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance, nor any rationale for changes, is present in the provided evidence.
No information is provided about changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains or rationales for such changes.

elements.quote: The primary outcome of this meta-analysis was to compute the pooled global prevalence of CAM. The secondary outcome was to compute the pooled prevalence of diabetes, steroid use, and mortality among CAM patients.
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies the primary outcome (pooled global prevalence of CAM), indicating which outcome is considered most important, but it does not provide an explicit rationale for prioritising this outcome over others.

elements.quote: Two independent reviewers (S.H. and H.B.) extracted the following information from all the eligible studies: study author, year, country, study period or duration, the number of COVID-19 cases, confirmation of COVID-19, the diagnosis of mucormycosis, the number of mucormycosis cases among COVID-19 patients, the presence of comorbidities, the mean age of mucormycosis patients, female (%), clinical symptoms, treatment modalities, and mortality. Any confusion in the data collection process was resolved by discussion with a third reviewer (M.K.).
elements.reason: The manuscript lists many 'other variables' extracted (author, year, country, study period, case counts, confirmation methods, diagnosis methods, comorbidities, age, sex %, symptoms, treatments, mortality), but it does not provide definitions or operational criteria for these variables (e.g., how comorbidities were categorized, how clinical symptoms were defined), so the requirement is only partially met.

No explicit description of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information (for example assumed values, imputation methods, or rules for interpreting unclear reports) is provided in the retrieved evidence.
The evidence does not cite any specific tool or framework used to determine which data items to collect (no data collection instrument or guidance document is referenced for selecting data items).

elements.quote: The JBI critical appraisal tool for studies reporting prevalence data was used to assess the quality assessment of the included studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly names the risk-of-bias tool used (JBI critical appraisal tool for prevalence studies).

elements.quote: This tool comprised nine questions dealing with the target population, sample size, condition measured, and statistical analysis with yes, no, unclear, and not applicable responses.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the domains/components of the tool (nine questions addressing target population, sample size, condition measured, statistical analysis) and the response options.

elements.quote: All the included studies were of high quality as per the assessment based on the JBI critical appraisal tool for prevalence studies.
elements.reason: An overall risk-of-bias judgement (studies rated as high quality) is reported, but the manuscript does not report the explicit rules or criteria used to derive that overall judgement.
No information is provided about any adaptations made to an existing risk-of-bias tool.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is described or made available in the provided evidence.
The manuscript does not state how many reviewers assessed risk of bias, whether they worked independently, or the procedures used to resolve disagreements for the risk-of-bias assessments.
No processes for contacting study investigators to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information are described in the provided evidence.
No automation tools used for risk-of-bias assessment (use, training, performance, validation) are described in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The pooled prevalence of mucormycosis among COVID-19 patients was computed.
elements.reason: The methods explicitly state that the pooled prevalence was computed for the outcome (i.e., prevalence is the effect measure used in the synthesis/presentation).
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes (for example, what constitutes a small/large prevalence) or rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence.
No methods describing re-expression of synthesized results using another effect measure were reported in the provided evidence.
The manuscript does not provide a justification for the choice of effect measure (prevalence) in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: All the articles were judged against the inclusion and exclusion parameters described in the eligibility criteria. The reviewers tried to resolve any confusion in the study selection process through discussion; if consensus was not reached by discussion, then the decision was made by consulting a third reviewer (M.K.).
elements.reason: The methods describe how studies were screened and judged against pre-specified inclusion and exclusion criteria, including independent screening by two reviewers, processes for resolving disagreements, and use of a third reviewer — detailing the process used to decide which studies were eligible for synthesis. Additional supporting evidence (text_13 and figure in text_15) shows that 15 full-text articles were assessed and six studies met inclusion for the meta-analysis, and the PRISMA flowchart (text_15) visually documents study selection counts.

The provided Methods and Statistical Analysis text describes software, pooled prevalence calculation, heterogeneity criteria, model choice, sensitivity and subgroup analyses, and GRADE assessment, but contains no description of any methods to prepare data for presentation or synthesis (for example, no procedures for handling missing summary statistics, no imputation methods, and no data conversions or transformations are reported).

elements.quote: Two independent reviewers (S.H. and H.B.) extracted the following information from all the eligible studies: study author, year, country, study period or duration, the number of COVID-19 cases, confirmation of COVID-19, the diagnosis of mucormycosis, the number of mucormycosis cases among COVID-19 patients, the presence of comorbidities, the mean age of mucormycosis patients, female (%), clinical symptoms, treatment modalities, and mortality.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the data items extracted from studies, which describes the content presented in tabular summaries (and a table of study characteristics and a risk-of-bias table is included).

elements.quote: Figure 3. Forest Plot of the Pooled Prevalence of Diabetes Mellitus among CAM Patients.
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies the use of forest plots (Figures 3–5) to display pooled prevalence results and notes that funnel plots and meta-regressions were not performed (text_12). However, it does not provide a methodological description of how these plots were constructed (e.g., plotting conventions, effect measure display, CIs) beyond naming them.
No text explicitly reports the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs (e.g., by year, sample size, risk of bias, or effect).
The manuscript uses standard graphical displays (forest plots) and does not report any non-standard graphs for which a rationale would be required; therefore this conditional item does not apply.

elements.quote: All statistical analyses were performed using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis software (CMA) version 2 (Biostat Inc., Englewood, NJ, USA).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the software and version used for statistical synthesis (CMA version 2).

elements.quote: Funnel plots and meta-regressions were not performed due to the limited number of included studies.
elements.reason: Although the authors state certain analyses were not performed, there is no description or justification of an alternative synthesis or summary method used when meta-analysis was not possible.

elements.quote: In the presence of significant heterogeneity, a meta-analysis was performed using a random effect model.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the model used for meta-analysis (random-effects when heterogeneity present) and gives a rationale tied to presence of heterogeneity; subgroup results also state use of a fixed effects model when I2 = 0% (text_18).

elements.quote: The pooled prevalence of CAM was found to be 0.70% (95% CI: 0.2-2.3%). Due to significantly high heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.6%), a meta-analysis was performed using a random effect analysis.
elements.reason: The statistical methods for synthesis are reported: random-effects meta-analysis for high heterogeneity and fixed-effects meta-analysis reported for subgroups with I2 = 0% (text_18 describes random effect; text_18 and text_18 (Diabetes Prevalence) note fixed effects).

elements.quote: Heterogeneity was identified if the I 2 statistics value was ≥ 50% or p < 0.10 based on the x 2 test for Cochran's Q statistics [61].
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the statistics used to identify heterogeneity (I2 and Cochran's Q / chi-squared test with thresholds).

elements.quote: In the presence of significant heterogeneity, a meta-analysis was performed using a random effect model.
elements.reason: While a random-effects model is stated, the manuscript does not report which between-study variance estimator (e.g., DerSimonian-Laird, REML) was used.

elements.quote: The pooled prevalence of CAM was found to be 0.70% (95% CI: 0.2-2.3%).
elements.reason: Confidence intervals are presented, but the manuscript does not describe the method used to calculate confidence intervals for the summary effect in the random-effects meta-analyses.

elements.quote: All statistical analyses were performed using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis software (CMA) version 2 (Biostat Inc., Englewood, NJ, USA).
elements.reason: No additional random-effects implementation details (e.g., weighting scheme, continuity corrections, transformation of proportions) are reported beyond stating the use of a random-effects model and the software.
No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed or described in the manuscript, so reporting of priors is not applicable.

elements.quote: A sensitivity analysis was performed using the leave-one-out method to assess if pooled effect estimates were influenced by any single study alone.
elements.reason: Although sensitivity analysis is described, there is no description of methods to account for statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study (e.g., multilevel models or robust variance estimation).

elements.quote: Funnel plots and meta-regressions were not performed due to the limited number of included studies.
elements.reason: The authors identify planned syntheses (funnel plots and meta-regressions) that were not performed and provide the reason (limited number of included studies).

elements.quote: Funnel plots and meta-regressions were not performed due to the limited number of included studies. A sensitivity analysis was performed using the leave-one-out method to assess if pooled effect estimates were influenced by any single study alone. The subgroup analysis was performed based on diabetes as a comorbidity, and steroid exposure.
elements.reason: The methods used to explore heterogeneity are described: subgroup analyses (by diabetes and steroid exposure) and a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis; meta-regression and funnel plots were explicitly not performed.

elements.quote: The subgroup analysis was performed based on diabetes as a comorbidity, and steroid exposure.
elements.reason: The factors used for subgroup analysis (diabetes, steroid exposure) are specified, but the evidence does not report factor levels or any expected direction of effect modification.
No information is provided on whether analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both.
No methods are reported for how subgroup effects were compared (no statistical tests or comparison approach described).
There is no description of informal methods used to explore heterogeneity when meta-analysis was unsuitable, nor factors/levels for such informal exploration.
The report does not identify which heterogeneity analyses (if any) were not pre-specified.

elements.quote: The present meta-analysis revealed that the pooled prevalence of CAM among hospitalised COVID-19 patients was 7 cases per 1000 patients. In their comprehensive review of fungal coinfections among COVID-19 cohorts, Peng et al. (2021) found that the pooled prevalence of all fungal coinfections was 12 cases per 1000 patients, with a statistically significant difference between Asian (15 cases per 1000 patients) and European populations (7 cases per 1000 patients) [65]. The pooled prevalence of COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (CAPA) was 6 cases per 1000 patients, which was slightly similar to what we have found in terms of CAM prevalence, and the difference between Asian (13 cases per 1000 patients) and European populations (0.1 cases per 1000 patients) was statistically significant [65]. In comparison with the background prevalence of mucormycosis in comorbid populations, the pooled prevalence of CAM was 50 times higher than the highest documented prevalence of mucormycosis that was among the diabetic patients in India (0.14 cases per 1000 patients) [20,66]. The pooled prevalence of diabetes mellitus among CAM patients was 74.5% which is similar to what had been previously reported in Mexico and Iran, where diabetes mellitus was a notable predisposing risk factor among mucormycosis patients with an overall prevalence of 72% and 75.4%, respectively [67,68].
elements.reason: The discussion directly compares the study's pooled prevalence estimates and comorbidity prevalences with prior systematic reviews and regional/background prevalence data, interpreting the results in the context of other evidence.
